name: Bianca Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and what you say is confidential. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head of livestock on the Ashgrove estate, which means three hundred and fifty beef cattle, plus I help with the potato harvest every autumn whether I like it or not. I start at six with the feed wagon, check the youngstock, then it's whatever's broken. I've got three people under me. The job comes with the cottage, so my husband Marco and I have lived in a house that isn't ours for nineteen years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what tires you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like calving, strange as it sounds. Two in the morning with a heifer having trouble, and you get the calf out and it stands up, there's nothing better. What tires me out is the new owner. Old Mr Hale ran the estate for forty years, now it's his son Julian, and Julian reads farming magazines on his phone and wants to try everything in them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there we are, and I'd mean it kindly. Nobody likes to hear I told you so. I'd probably say it to Marco over supper and leave it there, I don't go online for that sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means Julian finds another hobby and leaves my cattle alone. I'd be grateful, honestly. I've got about seven years before I'd want to stop, and I'd like them to be ordinary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd keep doing the job as I do it now, keep putting a bit away each month, we've got about four months saved. I wouldn't be learning any programs, I'd have no reason to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, I'd say, like a weight I didn't know I was carrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is Julian already trying AI or machines on the estate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's got a drone that flies over the potatoes and some app that tells him which field needs spraying. Fair play, it's probably useful for the potatoes. He's tried to give me collars for the cattle that send their temperature to his phone, and I've said I'll think about it, which means no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing big changes, how do you see your last working years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calving, feeding, shouting at Julian's drone. Then retiring at sixty-five and finding somewhere for me and Marco to live, because the cottage goes with the job. That part's always been at the back of my mind, AI or not.

S0.say: She'd say kindly to her husband over supper that it turned out as she thought, avoiding any gloating and not posting anything online.
S0.think: Privately it means the estate's new owner finds another hobby and leaves her cattle alone, giving her about seven ordinary years before she stops.
S0.do: Keeps doing the job as she does now and keeps saving a bit monthly, with about four months put by. Doesn't learn any AI programs because she sees no reason to.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved, like putting down a weight she hadn't noticed carrying.
S0.quote: He's tried to give me collars for the cattle that send their temperature to his phone, and I've said I'll think about it, which means no.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca is dry, private and quietly stubborn. Her tied cottage is a hidden stake in every scenario: losing the job means losing the house. She doesn't resent technology in general, only having it pushed onto her cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's good and bad in it, like most things. Some of it will help the young ones, and some people will get hurt. I'm not one for big opinions in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think Julian would be thrilled and I'd be the obstacle. He'd want the collars, the robot feeder, all of it. I'd be fifty-nine and the one who doesn't use the phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and wait to see what Julian actually buys before I panic. I'd put more away each month, maybe an extra hundred and fifty, because if things go wrong I need a deposit for somewhere to live. I'd let my deputy, Aled, deal with the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's the cottage, mostly. I can live with change at work, but not with losing the roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your job would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The feeding, I'd guess. There are wagons now that drive themselves along the feed barrier at set times. And the collars, which would mean Julian knows a cow's sick before I do, or thinks he does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'I'll think about it' means no. Could you keep saying no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while. I'm good at my job, Julian knows that, his father told him so. But I'm not daft, if the machines prove themselves, my no gets quieter every year.

S1.say: She'd say publicly there's good and bad in it, some people helped and some hurt, while avoiding strong opinions in public.
S1.think: Privately she thinks the new owner would be thrilled and she'd be the obstacle, the fifty-nine-year-old who doesn't use the phone.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and waits to see what the owner actually buys before reacting. Saves an extra hundred and fifty a month toward a house deposit and lets her deputy handle the machines.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mainly because her home depends on the job.
S1.quote: I'm not daft, if the machines prove themselves, my no gets quieter every year.
S1.fieldNote: Her centrist reluctance to take public positions contrasts with a very clear private read of her situation. She waits rather than fights, which fits her risk-averse style. The tied cottage turns ordinary job worry into something more basic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and somebody should have seen it coming, the government or the companies or someone. But I'd say it quietly. I'm not one for marches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out within a year or so. Julian would buy a robot herd system on finance and keep one young lad to watch the screens. And then the cottage goes, and we're fifty-nine with four months of money and nowhere to live.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything at once: no holidays, Marco sells his second car, we stop eating out on Fridays. I'd look at renting a small place in town before I was pushed, so we're not desperate. I'd ask our daughters whether we could stay with one of them for a bit if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I wouldn't sleep, I know I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the cottage in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It goes with the job, so it goes. Julian would maybe give us six months, he's not cruel. But six months in a world where every farm is doing the same thing, there'd be no other cottage going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco first, then our eldest, Sofia. She's got a spare room and a husband who'd put up with us. I'd hate it, but I'd do it.

S2.say: She'd say quietly that it came too fast and someone, whether government or companies, should have seen it coming, but she wouldn't march or campaign.
S2.think: Privately she expects to be out within a year as the owner buys a robotic herd system, and losing the job means losing the cottage at fifty-nine with four months of savings.
S2.do: Cuts spending at once, dropping holidays, a second car and Friday meals out. Looks at renting a small place in town before being pushed and asks her daughters if they could stay with one of them.
S2.quote: And then the cottage goes, and we're fifty-nine with four months of money and nowhere to live.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her life could unravel, because her job, her home and her income all hang on one employer. She doesn't blame the owner personally and doesn't turn to politics. Family is her safety net, though using it would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a bit of time, let's be sensible about it. I'd tell the younger ones on the estate to learn the machines. I'd keep my own counsel about my own plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, five years gets me to sixty-three. That's close to stopping anyway. If I can get a deposit together, the cottage problem becomes a moving problem, not a disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save hard, about a quarter of my wage, to put down a deposit on a small house in town within four years. I'd ask Julian for a written promise on notice for the cottage. And I'd keep working the old way as long as he'd let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I had a plan. It's a race I might win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With five years, what changes about the cottage problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything. Five years is a deposit. Two years is a sofa at my daughter's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years make you try the collars or the screens, to stay useful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I'd rather work fewer years my way than more years staring at Julian's phone. I know that's stubborn, Marco tells me so most weeks.

S3.say: She'd say there's a bit of time so people should be sensible, encouraging younger estate workers to learn the machines while keeping her own plans private.
S3.think: Privately five years gets her to sixty-three, close to stopping, and if she can save a deposit the cottage problem becomes a moving problem rather than a disaster.
S3.do: Saves about a quarter of her wage toward a deposit on a small house in town within four years. Asks the owner for a written promise on notice for the cottage and keeps working her way as long as she's allowed.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with a plan and a race she thinks she might win.
S3.quote: Five years is a deposit. Two years is a sofa at my daughter's.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years transform her situation because they let her secure housing. She still refuses to adapt at work, preferring a shorter career on her own terms. The contrast between two and five years is starker for her than for most, because of the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, people should plan, and the government should make sure there's help for the young ones. That's about as political as I get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be retired by then. I'd want to be out at sixty-five anyway, in our own little house. It'd be Aled and the youngsters who face it, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, saving steadily and buying a small house in town with Marco by about sixty-two, renting it out until we move in. I'd retire at sixty-five as planned. I wouldn't change how I work with the cattle at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but only a little, and more for the youngsters than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years would take you past sixty-five. Does this one touch you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, if things go to plan. It'd be like the slow change one for me, just far enough off that I've stopped by the time it bites.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing the year before it arrives, around 2035?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Living in town, in our own house for the first time in thirty years. Probably driving out to Ashgrove now and then to see the calves and grumble about how the robots are doing it.

S4.say: She'd say ten years is plenty, people should plan and the government should make sure young people get help, which is as political as she gets.
S4.think: Privately she expects to be retired by then in their own small house, with her deputy and younger workers facing it instead of her.
S4.do: Carries on as she is, saving steadily and buying a small house in town by about sixty-two, renting it out until they move in. Retires at sixty-five as planned without changing how she works with the cattle.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, more for the younger workers than for herself.
S4.quote: Living in town, in our own house for the first time in thirty years.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, she is mostly safe and her plan is almost unchanged from the plateau. The house remains the centre of her thinking in every scenario. She shows quiet concern for younger colleagues without taking any public stance.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of the cottage. What would help is a rule that if a farm job comes with a house, you can't be put out of it for a machine without a year's notice and some money toward somewhere else. That's not much to ask.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether we're asked at all. Nobody asked me about the drone. I'd have said yes to the drone, probably, if anyone had bothered to ask.

headlineQuote: I'd have said yes to the drone, probably, if anyone had bothered to ask.
portrait: Bianca Garcia, 58, is head of livestock on a private estate, running a beef herd with three staff, and she and her husband live in a cottage that comes with the job. She's private, dry and firmly against using AI tools herself, and she holds pragmatic, middle-of-the-road views she rarely airs in public. Her biggest stake in every scenario is the house: AGI in two years alarms her because job and home would go together. With five or ten years she turns to saving for a deposit and planning to retire to her own place in town.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years worries her most, because losing her job would also mean losing the tied cottage with only a few months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A rule that workers in job-linked homes get a year's notice and money toward new housing if replaced by a machine.
